title: How to Measure Your App’s Visibility in AI Search
summary: Build a repeatable process to track your app's AI mentions, recommendations, and citations, then connect the findings to traffic and business outcomes.
body_markdown:
Many teams check their AI visibility by asking ChatGPT about their app once, reading the answer, and moving on. One response tells you very little. Ask the same question again, in another assistant, or next week, and the shortlist can change.


A more useful approach is to run a fixed set of prompts, repeat them, and record what comes back. That’s the method An Nayal, founder of the couples app Flamme, described on Tenjin’s ROI 101 podcast with Roman Garbar: real user prompts, several AI engines, repeated runs, and a record of who’s named and who’s cited.


This guide turns that method into a baseline you can run yourself. The definitions, tracking table, and formulas are our editorial additions to An’s approach, so you can compare results over time.


**Key Takeaways**


- Measure mentions, recommendations, and citations separately. They tell you different things.
- Start with around 10 prompts based on real customer language. An’s larger process uses 50 prompts, 4 engines, and 3 runs each: 600 responses per pass.
- Record the conditions of every run. Results describe only the prompts and conditions you tested.
- Keep answer visibility, referral traffic, paid AI traffic, and business outcomes as separate views.


## Define What You Are Measuring


AI search visibility for an app is how often, and how accurately, the app appears in AI-generated answers to a defined set of prompts. To measure it, separate three outcomes:


- **Mention:** the response names your app.
- **Recommendation:** the response suggests your app as a fit for the person’s need. Write your definition down, for example “named in the top three with a reason that fits the prompt”, and use it every time.
- **Citation:** the response links to a URL as a source.


A response can mention your app without recommending it, or recommend it without citing your website.


Separate your prompts by type, too. These examples are illustrative, for a habit-tracking app:


**Prompt type** **Example** **What it tells you**


Problem-based “How can I stick to a morning routine?” Whether you appear before someone has thought of an app


Category “Best habit tracker apps for iPhone” Whether you make the shortlist


Branded “Does \[Your App\] have an Apple Watch app?” Whether the facts about your app are accurate


Observed visibility applies only to the prompts and conditions you tested. It isn’t a universal position in AI search.


## Choose Prompts for User Decisions


The simplest starting point is a small set of prompts your users would actually type. As An puts it:


> *What they could do is pick 10 prompts their buyers would type, run them in GPT, and write down who’s named and who’s cited, right?*


Start with the questions, not the fixes. Many teams jump straight to asking an AI to rewrite their website. An’s point is that “you need to know what AI is being asked first.” For a couples app, his examples are problem-based prompts such as “What is the best app for my relationship?” or “What can I use with my partner?”, not the app’s name.


Build your prompts from real customer language:


- Phrases from app reviews and support tickets
- Questions people ask before installing or subscribing
- Your main use cases and audiences
- Search queries that already bring visitors to your website


Cover five prompt categories in your starting set:


1. Best app for a specific problem
2. App for a specific audience
3. Comparison between two options
4. A pricing or feature requirement
5. A branded fact check


Ten prompts give you a directional baseline, not a statistically representative sample. Report branded fact checks separately. Branded prompts are easy to “win”, and mixing them in would inflate your discovery results.


## Do Repeat Checks for Visibility Baseline


AI answers vary between runs, so one check isn’t enough. An’s rule is that “the thing that never lies is volume”, and his process repeats every prompt:


> *We run all the prompts on four engines, three times each, with live search* .


At the scale An described, that’s 50 prompts across ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and Gemini, 3 runs each: 50 x 4 x 3 = 600 responses per complete pass. Three repetitions show you how much answers vary. They don’t establish a definitive rank.


An explains why three runs matter:


> *What that helps us understand is one result could be an outlier, two results maybe not true, but once we do it three times, we really understand, okay, what is the truth?*


Which engines should you check? For consumer apps, An’s rule of thumb is short:


> *optimize for GPT, measure all four.*


**[SE Ranking’s 2026 study of AI referral traffic](https://seranking.com/blog/ai-traffic)** backs this up: ChatGPT sent 74.78% of AI referral visits to websites, followed by Gemini (11.56%), Perplexity (7.23%), Copilot (3.51%), and Claude (2.62%). ChatGPT’s share is falling as the other assistants grow faster, which is why it’s worth measuring more than one engine.


For every run, record:


- The exact prompt text
- The date
- The engine, and the model where it’s visible
- The search mode, such as live web search on or off
- Language and market
- Session conditions: a fresh session, signed out where possible, with memory and custom instructions off
- The repetition number


Use the same session setup for every baseline, because memory, personalization, and location can all change answers. Without tooling, An suggests spreading the runs across people: “they could have them run like three prompts, their friend run three prompts, their colleague run three prompts.” Different accounts add variety, so record whose session each run used and keep those runs apart from your fresh-session baseline.


An’s team analyzes its tracker week on week. For a small team running checks by hand, a monthly pass is a realistic start, moving to weekly while you’re actively changing your website or listings. Set the cadence your resources can sustain.


## Use a Tracking Table That Separates Outcomes


Copy this table into a spreadsheet and log one row per response:


**Field** **What to record**


Prompt ID and intent Exact wording and the user decision being tested


Engine and conditions Date, search mode, language, market, and repetition


App mentioned Yes or no


App recommended Yes or no, using your written definition


Evidence URL cited Your own page, your store listing, or an external source


Competitors named Which alternatives appeared


Accuracy Incorrect pricing, features, platform support, or positioning


Action The information gap, the page to fix, an owner, and the next review date


## Calculate a Small Set of Comparable Metrics


Three rates are enough to compare engines, prompt groups, and periods:


- **Mention rate** = valid responses naming the app ÷ valid responses tested
- **Recommendation rate** = valid responses recommending the app ÷ valid responses tested
- **Citation rate** (for a defined set of URLs) = valid responses citing at least one URL in that set ÷ valid responses tested


Here’s an illustrative example. You run 10 prompts across 4 engines, 3 times each: 120 responses. Four runs fail, leaving 116 valid responses.


**Metric** **Count** **Rate**


Mention rate 29 of 116 25.0%


Recommendation rate 17 of 116 14.7%


Citation rate, your domain 9 of 116 7.8%


A few rules keep these numbers honest:


- Report rates by engine and by intent group, not only as one total.
- Report citations of your domain, your store listings, and third-party sources separately.
- Keep the same prompt set for trend comparisons, and note any change to it.
- Count failed runs separately rather than dropping them silently.
- Don’t translate these rates into a share of all AI queries or into market demand. They describe your sample.


## Turn Cited Sources and Factual Errors Into Actions


The citations in your tracking table show which sources AI engines rely on for your category. As An puts it:


> *You should do an AI search to find what the top sources are.*


In other words, look at the sources actually cited in your sampled answers rather than assuming they match Google’s top results. Then map each finding to an action:


**Finding** **Action**


Wrong price, features, or platform support Fix it on your website and listings, then check third-party pages repeating the error


A use case you serve is never mentioned Add a clear section or page for it


Competitors win comparison prompts Improve your comparison and fit information, honestly


A frequently cited publication doesn’t include you Approach it with relevant, accurate evidence


Your own page is cited but has no clear download link Add a download button with a tracked link, so visits from AI answers can be followed to the install


Our guide to[GEO for mobile apps](https://tenjin.com/blog/blog-geo-for-mobile-apps/) covers how to fix each of these across your store listings, website, reviews, and external coverage.


Log every change with its date. If visibility shifts later, that’s an observation, not proof that one edit caused it.


## Connect AI Visibility to Traffic and Business Results


AI visibility, website traffic, paid AI traffic, and app revenue are different measurements. Keep them in separate views:


**View** **What it shows** **Where the data comes from**


Sampled answer visibility Mentions, recommendations, and citations in your prompt set Your tracking table


Identifiable referral traffic Visits from AI assistants that pass a referrer Web analytics, for example referrals from chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai


Paid AI traffic Installs and in-app events from ChatGPT Ads clicks Your attribution platform, through its tracking link in the campaign


Business outcomes Sign-ups, installs, activation, subscriptions, and revenue Attribution and product analytics


A citation doesn’t mean a click, and a click doesn’t mean an install. When someone reads an AI answer then searches the App Store directly, it’s hard to connect the two. For Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode, traffic is counted within overall Search traffic in Search Console, so it can’t be separated there.


## Catch AI-Assisted Installs That Look Organic


Two kinds of AI-assisted installs usually end up in the wrong place. Clicks from AI answers that arrive without a tag or referrer show up as direct, and people who read an answer and then search the store by name show up as organic. These steps recover part of both:


- **Report on AI tags and referrers:** ChatGPT often adds utm_source=chatgpt.com to the links in its answers. Report on that tag, and group referrers such as chatgpt.com, gemini.google.com, perplexity.ai, copilot.microsoft.com, and claude.ai into one AI channel in your web analytics, so untagged visits still count.
- **Carry the tag through to your store links:** pass tracking parameters from your landing page into the download button. Otherwise a visit from an AI answer followed by a download is recorded as organic.
- **Give every cited page a download path:** the pages AI answers cite should each have a clear, tracked link to your store listing.
- **Ask new users how they found you:** add “An AI assistant” as an option in a “How did you hear about us?” onboarding question. It catches installs that started with an answer and no click.
- **Watch store search installs:** App Store Connect and Google Play Console both report installs from store search, and Play Console shows the search terms. A rise in searches for your app’s name as your visibility improves is a signal, not proof.
- **Judge AI users on value:** people who research before installing often convert later, so compare day 7 and day 30 revenue by source, not only install counts. Our[user acquisition strategy guide](https://tenjin.com/blog/blog-app-user-acquisition-strategy/) covers looking past day-7 ROAS.


What you can do is measure the outcomes you can attribute.[Tenjin’s mobile attribution](https://tenjin.com/mobile-attribution/) shows installs, revenue, and ROI by source, so you can see whether organic growth moves alongside your visibility work, and compare it with paid channels. Tenjin doesn’t track AI citations. It does attribute installs and in-app events from ChatGPT Ads, so paid AI traffic sits next to your other channels. Installs from people who read an answer and then search the store by name can’t be traced back to that answer, which is why the steps above matter.


If social content drives people to research your app later, An’s view on[connecting TikTok and AI search](https://tenjin.com/blog/organic-user-acquisition-tiktok-ai-search/) explains how the two work together.


## Frequently Asked Questions


****How do I check whether ChatGPT recommends my app?****


To check whether ChatGPT recommends your app, run a fixed set of prompts your users would type, in a fresh session with live search on, three times each. Record whether your app is mentioned, recommended, and cited, and repeat the same check in other assistants your audience uses.


****Why do answers differ when I repeat the same prompt?****


AI answers differ between runs because responses are generated rather than retrieved from a fixed ranking, and live search results, model versions, location, and session context can change. Repeating each prompt shows how stable your visibility is.


****How many prompts should I monitor?****


Around 10 prompts is a practical starting set for a small team. An Nayal, founder of Flamme, describes a larger process of 50 prompts across four engines, three times each. Choose a set you can run consistently, and keep branded prompts separate.


****What is the difference between a mention and a citation?****


A mention is when an AI answer names your app. A citation is when the answer links to a page as a source, such as your website, your store listing, or a third-party review. An app can be mentioned without being cited, and a page can be cited without the app being recommended.


****Can AI visibility be connected to app installs and revenue?****


AI visibility can be connected to app installs and revenue only partly. Referral visits from some AI assistants are identifiable in web analytics, and attribution tools measure installs and revenue by source, but many AI-assisted journeys can’t be traced end to end. Track visibility, traffic, and outcomes as separate views.


****How do I track app installs from ChatGPT Ads?****


To track app installs from ChatGPT Ads, connect your attribution platform to ChatGPT Ads, use its tracking link in the campaign, and map the in-app events you want to send back. Attribution for ChatGPT Ads is click-based, so people who saw an ad but didn’t click it won’t be credited to the campaign.


****Why does AI traffic show up as direct or organic?****


AI traffic shows up as direct when a link from an AI answer arrives with no tag and no referrer, and as organic when someone reads an answer and then searches the app store by name. Grouping AI referrers, carrying tags through to your store links, and asking new users how they found you recover part of both.


**Ready to start?** Copy the tracking table, pick your first 10 prompts, and run a baseline this week. When you’re ready to see which channels bring installs and revenue, then it’s time to explore[Tenjin’s mobile attribution](https://tenjin.com/mobile-attribution/) .
